Where Valley Fever risk is highest in California

Valley Fever comes from a fungus that lives in dry soil. We mapped the whole state to find the areas whose climate looks like the places where this illness is already common, as a first step toward protecting people who work outdoors.

In short

Certain parts of California have the hot, dry conditions this fungus needs. Those areas are concentrated in the San Joaquin Valley and the inner Central Coast, and they account for most of the illness reported in the state. The map below lets you look up any county or city.

4.0 millionCalifornians live where the climate closely matches known Valley Fever areas, roughly 1 in 10 residents
54%of reported cases come from the five counties the model ranks highest, home to just 6% of the population
85 out of 100times the model correctly picked the affected place when shown two locations it had never seen
Dry summersturned out to be the strongest signal, ahead of heat

What Valley Fever is

A lung infection you get from breathing dust, not from other people.

Valley Fever is caused by a fungus that lives in soil in parts of California. When dry ground gets disturbed, spores can rise into the air and people nearby breathe them in. It does not spread from person to person.

Most people who breathe in spores never feel sick. Others develop symptoms resembling the flu or pneumonia, sometimes lasting weeks or months, and a small number become seriously ill. Because the spores travel in dust, the highest exposure tends to fall on people who disturb soil for a living, including construction and farm work. California reported about 9,000 cases in 2023, and preliminary counts for 2024 were the highest on record.

Read this before using the map

The model view does not show where the fungus has been found in the ground. Almost no one has tested California soil for it. What it shows is where conditions look right, based on the climate of places where people already get sick. Treat it as a screening tool for deciding where to look closer, not as a hazard assessment for any particular address.

What drives the risk

The model could draw on seven climate and terrain measurements. Two did nearly all the work.

High-ranked areas carry a disproportionate share of illness

The strongest evidence that it picks up something real is that the places it ranks highest account for most of the state's illness, even though very few people live there.

Dry summers are the strongest environmental signal

The clear winner is how dry it gets in the driest part of the year. Second is how cold winter nights get, since mild winters help. Total yearly rainfall and elevation barely mattered on their own. That fits what is known about this fungus, which survives hot dry stretches that other soil organisms cannot, then releases spores as the ground dries. An independent study of the same disease in northeastern Brazil reached the same conclusion, finding rainfall rather than temperature to be the key driver.

How we tested it

A map that only describes the data it was built from is worthless, so we ran three separate checks.

1. Hide whole regions

We split the state into blocks, hid a quarter of them, rebuilt the map from the rest, then scored the hidden areas. Repeated until every block had a turn.

Correct 85 times out of 100

2. Hide an entire county

Harder. We removed one known affected county completely, as if it had never been studied, and checked whether the model could still recognize it.

Worked for 6 of 7 counties

3. Compare with real records

We compared each county's score against 23 years of reported cases, including 51 counties that played no part in building the model.

Higher scoring counties report more illness

The one failure is more informative than the six successes. San Luis Obispo is coastal, cooler and wetter than the inland farming counties, and a model taught on the hot dry San Joaquin Valley does not recognize it. That tells us the coast is a genuinely different situation and needs its own treatment.

What this map cannot tell you

  • Not when. It shows places where risk is generally elevated year after year. It says nothing about whether today is a dusty, high risk day. Timing is the next phase and needs different data.
  • Not a specific address. Each square is roughly 3 miles across, and soil and land use vary a great deal within that.
  • It does not detect the fungus. It reads climate, not the ground.
  • It partly reflects where people get diagnosed. We built it from records of who got sick, because almost no soil testing data exists. Places with more testing, more clinical awareness, or more workers disturbing soil can look riskier for reasons that are not purely environmental.
  • It misses the coast, as the hidden county test showed.
  • About 6 percent of the state has a climate unlike anywhere the model studied, so scores there sit at the edge of what it knows.

Suitable ground is not the same as risk to people

San Benito County scores near the top of the state, yet only about 5 percent of its residents live on that suitable land, so its case counts stay low. Risk to people appears where suitable ground and human activity overlap, and finding that overlap is the point of the next phase.

Next steps

  1. Add timing, using month by month weather and especially rainfall from the previous winter, which research links to how many people get sick the following year.
  2. Add satellite measurements of dust, soil moisture and vegetation, which would move this toward telling us when dust is actually flying.
  3. Request neighborhood level illness data from public health, which would break the circular reasoning that is this model's main weakness.
  4. Overlay workplaces, combining risky ground with where people actually work outdoors. That is the piece that would make this operational for Cal/OSHA.

Technical details

For reviewers. Everything below is reproducible from the published code.

Method and settings

Maximum Entropy species distribution model (MaxEnt) via elapid and maxnet, cloglog output, linear, quadratic, hinge and product features, regularization multiplier chosen by sweep (1.0, stable across 1 to 4).

Reference locations: 323 grid cells holding population weighted census tract centroids inside the seven counties whose pooled 2001 to 2023 incidence reaches 20 per 100,000, the statutory threshold in Labor Code 6709 (AB 203). Weighting by population keeps reference points on inhabited valley floor rather than uninhabited mountains in the same counties.

Comparison locations: 2314 cells covering all California tract centroids, a target group background that corrects for illness being observed only where people are. Predictors are WorldClim 2.1 bioclimatic variables plus elevation at 2.5 arc minutes, pruned to Spearman correlation below 0.7, leaving seven. Population is never a predictor.

Performance
MeasureValuePlain meaning
AUC, spatial block cross validation0.851Ranks a held out affected and unaffected location correctly about 85% of the time
AUC, training0.926Performance on data it studied. The gap is the honest cost of real testing
AUC, leave one county out0.821Six of seven counties above 0.85, San Luis Obispo 0.24
Spearman correlation, 51 held out counties0.453The defensible independent figure
Spearman correlation, all 580.62Partly circular, since seven counties defined the reference set
Novel environment6.3%Share of the state outside the training climate range

The Brazilian study reported 0.87 but did not report spatially blocked validation, so the fair comparison is with our training figure of 0.926 rather than the more conservative 0.851.

Supporting figures
Weaknesses a reviewer should press on
  • Circularity. Reference locations came from illness data and validation uses illness data. Holding out 51 counties and strict county transfer tests reduce this but do not remove it.
  • County boundaries are not ecological. A county level threshold labels every tract alike.
  • Ascertainment and occupational confounding. Documented institutional outbreaks and heavy agricultural and construction exposure in the Central Valley raise recorded incidence in ways this design cannot separate from climate.
  • Static climate averages describe habitat but cannot express the year to year swings that drive case surges.

Status: research preview prepared for internal review. This is not an official health advisory and carries no regulatory force.

Cal/OSHA publishes guidance on reducing Valley Fever exposure at work. Anyone with a lasting cough, fever or fatigue after dust exposure should mention Valley Fever to a clinician, since it is often mistaken for ordinary pneumonia.
